content: The Social Skills Improvement System Rating Scale and the Pictorial Scale of Perceived Competence and Social Acceptance for Young Children were used to objectively measure all outcomes. In one randomized controlled trial (RCT) with 226 participants, no eligible reviews were identified. There was a serious risk of bias, and the data could not be assessed for inconsistency. However, there was no serious indirectness or imprecision. The study found no effect of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) on time spent in play or social skills (Bundy et al., 2017). The quality of evidence was downgraded to low. In one non-randomized trial (NRT) with 1,322 participants, no eligible reviews were identified. There was a serious risk of bias, and inconsistency could not be assessed. However, there was no serious indirectness or imprecision. The study reported positive effects of MVPA on effort and time on task (Carlson et al., 2015). The quality of evidence was downgraded to very low. In one longitudinal study with 7,704 participants, no eligible reviews were identified. There was a serious risk of bias, and inconsistency could not be assessed. However, there was no serious indirectness or imprecision. The study found that physical activity (PA) was associated with fewer peer problems. However, MVPA was unfavorably associated with conduct and hyperactivity problems in both boys and girls, and with conduct problems in boys only (Ahn et al., 2018). The quality of evidence was downgraded to very low. In one cross-sectional study with 652 participants, no eligible reviews were identified. There was a serious risk of bias, and inconsistency could not be assessed. However, there was no serious indirectness or imprecision. The study found no association between total PA and prosocial behavior, peer problems, social acceptance, or conduct problems in boys or girls (Sebire et al., 2011). However, MVPA was favorably correlated with peer problems and social acceptance in boys (but not girls) and with prosocial behavior in girls (but not boys). MVPA was not associated with conduct problems in either boys or girls. The quality of evidence was downgraded to very low. Abbreviations: MVPA: Moderate-to-vigorous physical activity PA: Physical activity The quality of evidence from the RCT was downgraded from high to low due to a serious risk of bias and inability to assess inconsistency. The quality of evidence from the NRT was downgraded from low to very low for similar reasons. The longitudinal study's evidence could not be upgraded from low to moderate due to a serious risk of bias and was further downgraded to very low because inconsistency could not be assessed. The cross-sectional study's evidence was also downgraded from low to very low due to a serious risk of bias and inability to assess inconsistency. Regarding sleep duration and quality in children and adolescents, the association between PA and health-related outcomes was explored. Questions included whether there is a dose-response relationship (volume, duration, frequency, intensity) and whether the association varies by type or domain of PA. The population studied included children aged 5–18 years. The exposure was greater PA, and the comparison was less or no PA. The outcome of interest was sleep duration and quality. This was deemed an important area of study, but no systematic reviews were identified by the WHO. For physical fitness and sedentary behavior in children and adolescents, the association between sedentary behavior and health-related outcomes was examined. Questions included whether there is a dose-response relationship (total volume, frequency, duration, intensity of interruption) and whether the association varies by type or domain of sedentary behavior. Fitness was assessed using various objective measures, including cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF), flexibility, muscular strength/endurance, and power. Higher sedentary behavior was associated with lower fitness levels across multiple domains, including CRF, muscular strength, and flexibility, as measured by accelerometer-derived sedentary time, screen time, TV viewing, and video game use. The quality of evidence ranged from moderate to low, depending on the study design and outcome. For cardiometabolic health and sedentary behavior in children and adolescents, the association between sedentary behavior and health-related outcomes was also explored. Questions included whether there is a dose-response relationship and whether the association varies by type or domain of sedentary behavior. Cardiometabolic risk factors assessed included blood pressure (BP), lipid profiles, glucose, insulin resistance, and inflammatory markers. Higher sedentary behavior was associated with higher clustered risk scores and adverse cardiometabolic outcomes, particularly for screen time and TV viewing. The quality of evidence was generally low to very low, with mixed results observed across studies.
